div.p: Emerging trends in applications with the requirement of considerable computational capacity and decreasing time-tomarket have urged the need of multiprocessor systems. With the advent of multiprocessor systems, there is an increased demand to efficiently control their energy and power budget. As the technology scales to increasingly smaller feature sizes, the static power consumption is expected to grow exponentially which will also contribute a significant part in system's total power consumption. Moreover, modern-day applications are complex and offer limited extractable parallelism which eventually leads to poor performance by existing energy optimization techniques. In this paper, we present a two-fold framework for energy optimization. In the first step, we provide an algorithm, called MPSched (Minimum Processors for Schedulability), to optimize on the number of processors needed to fulfill execution requirement of target application. In the second step, we perform Static Voltage and Frequency Scaling (SVFS) to achieve an optimal energy profile of the system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Total power consumption in multiprocessor system-on-chip (MPSoC) is mainly composed of dynamic and static power components. The first relates to the power that is dissipated due to switching activity, while the second one is due to leakage currents. Energy optimization, while dealing exclusively with both these components, has been investigated by a significant number of researchers in recent years like [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8]. Until now, the most common way to reduce the total power consumption in MPSoCs is to schedule an application on as many processors as possible and apply frequency and voltage scaling afterwards. This is because frequency and voltage scaling techniques work only with dynamic component of power consumption which dominates static power consumption in current and past technologies. However, increasing trend in reduced feature sizes has started limiting the possibility of employing unlimited processors and consequently, limits the scaling of frequency and voltage as the leakage current is expected to increase exponentially [1] which will eventually increase static power consumption. Moreover, modern-day applications for MPSoC such as image & voice data processing, telecommunication protocols etc. are very complex and offer limited extractable parallelism. Therefore, increasing the number of processors in MPSoC or applying frequency and voltage scaling is constrained by technology in one way or the other. Hence, such solutions are not necessarily the stand-alone optimal solutions for energy consumption optimization. There is a need of a pragmatic approach to deal with the power consumption issues in current and future MPSoCs. In this paper, we present a multifold strategy to optimize overall energy consumption through offline profiling of MPSoCs. In the first step, we present an algorithm called MPSched (Minimum Processors for Schedulability) to determine the minimum effective number of processors needed to fulfill the execution requirement of an application. This algorithm determines the schedulability of tasks (of target application) at nominal frequency. Second step is an iterative process. Starting from the minimum number of processors determined in 1 st step, the operating frequency and supply voltage is scaled to obtain different energy profiles. An optimal energy profile can be selected then based on the operating conditions and available platform resources. Our objective in this study is to provide a framework which permits to apply energy optimization techniques at different levels. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section-II, we briefly describe some related research. In Section-III, we define the system model and some additional useful notations. In Section-IV we present our strategy in detail. In Section-V, we provide our experimental results. In Section-VI, we conclude our paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Researchers have analyzed both dynamic and static power consumption components exclusively. To deal with dynamic component of power, one of the most promising techniques that have been proposed is Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS), where both frequency and supply voltage are scaled down relative to the work load of scheduler [4,5]. Authors in [6] propose a similar approach to statically scale down the voltage and frequency of processors. The Approach presented in [7] determines a priori (offline) a suitable combination of voltage and frequency at which each real-time task shall execute while considering worstcase execution time (WCET). Our strategy for offline energy consumption optimization is closer to the one presented in [8] which aims at determining minimum operating frequency for identical multiprocessor system. The difference in our approach relative to [8] is that we do not fix the total number of processors in architecture a priori and therefore, the impact of static power consumption of processors and associated memory are the parameters taken into consideration.

div.head: IV. ENERGY OPTIMIZATION FRAMEWORK
div.p: We present a two-fold strategy for statically optimizing the energy consumption of MPSoCs. We consider that the number of processors in system is not known a priori. This consideration leads to the fact that static power consumption of processors and associated memories, along with the dynamic power consumption, will be significant parameter to take into account for determining the optimal energy profile of system. Our strategy eventually results in an optimal MPSoC architecture configuration, composed of number of processors (determined in first step) and corresponding operating frequency and supply voltage (determined in second step) under the constraints of a given degree of extractable parallelism in application and deadline guarantees. Fig. 1 shows various energy profiles of an MPSoC.

div.head: A. Step-1: Minimum Processors for Schedulability (MPSched)
div.p: MPSched is an admission control technique for globally scheduled tasks. It decides when a ready task should enter in running tasks' queue of the scheduler. Without this admission control, all ready tasks are executed as soon as there are enough computing resources available in the system leading to poor possibilities of putting some processors in low power state. For real time applications the worst-case (offline) underutilization ( ) ( )

div.p: execution, this under-utilization appears in the form of fragmented idle intervals. These idle intervals are non-stationary and occur randomly (at runtime) on different processors. This fragmentation in idle intervals is mainly because of tasks' run time parameters. MPSched extracts this fragmented idleness from some processors and clusters it on some other processor(s). Doing so permits to increase the length of idle interval and allows some k-processors to be in inactive state during these intervals while other (m-k) processors execute the existing and upcoming jobs of ready tasks. MPSched does not make assumptions about the form of the distribution governing the length of idle intervals which allows MPSched to adapt at runtime to non-stationary idle intervals in various application models. We consider Earliest Deadline First global scheduling policy to demonstrate how MPSched works.

MPSched takes into account c i l of all released tasks and analyzes whether it is possible to delay the execution of some low priority tasks in order to use the same number of processor(s) which are currently executing higher priority task(s) or not? If so, then these low priority tasks are deferred till the next scheduling event and remaining processors are either put in inactive state (if they were already in active state) or at least no further processor is activated. Otherwise, if a task cannot be deferred then a processor is put into active state to meet the execution requirement. The working principle is briefly described in Algorithm-I.

Example-1: Let's consider three periodic independent and synchronous tasks ( 1 τ , 2 τ , and 3 τ ) to be scheduled on two processors ( 1 π and 2 π ). The quadruplet values for tasks are ( 0, 3, 8, 8 ), ( 0, 6,1 0,1 0 ) and ( 0, 4,16,16 ) respectively. Fig. 3 (a) represents the EDF global schedule for these tasks. It can be noticed that, on run time, EDF generates some random idle intervals (gray dashed area) because of the under-utilization present in the schedule. Fig. 3 (b) shows the same schedule again where MPSched has extracted these idle time intervals from processor first processor and clustered them on second processor. These clustered idle time intervals can be used to put second processor in an energy efficient state for long time while first processor continues to execute released jobs at the nominal frequency.

div.head: B. Step-2: Static Voltage and Frequency Scaling (SVFS)
div.p: Optimizing only on the number of processors will not necessarily result in a better energy consumption profile of the system. Therefore, after step-1, we propose to statically scale down the operating frequency (F op ) and supply voltage (V dd ) to further reduce energy consumption. We refer this couple of parameters as (V dd , F op ) hereafter. It is important to note that scaling (V dd , F op ) may increase the number of processors used to meet deadlines but eventually result in a better energy profile. The question is; how many processors have to be included in the architecture and what suitable couple of (V dd , F op ) parameters shall be set up to these processors such that deadlines of tasks are met and energy consumption is minimized. To answer this question, we determine various energy consumption profiles of system by scaling (V dd , F op ) to all discrete operating points. An energy profile consists of two elements: a) the number of processors being used, i.e. m act b) a value for (V dd , F op ) couple. We recall from Eq. 1 that static power is a function of supply voltage V dd and leakage current. Static power decreases while V dd is decreasing until a limit where it rises again because of the fact that when V dd approaches threshold voltage V th , the leakage current starts increasing. Moreover, while scaling down (V dd , F op ) the number of processors may increase and multiplies with the static power component. Hence, the impact of static power consumption becomes significant as the number of processors (and their associated memories) increases. We have taken this into account and our experiments show some interesting results. Simulation results -Fig. 4 shows EDF schedule of tasks with idle time slots being extracted from 1 π and 2 π and clustered on 3 π by MPSched algorithm. We observe that for the given task set, MPSched uses at most three processors (m=3) at reference frequency to provide deadline guarantees. Once the minimum number of processors is determined, we statically scale down (in simulation) the operating frequency and supply voltage and iterate through all supported switching points (Fig. 5). We obtain a different energy profile (number of processors used, corresponding energy value) for every switching point (Table -3).

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper presents a two-fold energy consumption optimization framework. In first step, an algorithm called MPSched is presented which determines the minimum number of processors needed to fulfill the execution requirement of released jobs at runtime at reference frequency F ref . This algorithm extracts the fragmented idleness from an application's schedule which permits to increase the length of idle interval and allows some k-processors to be in energy efficient state during these intervals while other (m-k) processors execute the existing and upcoming jobs of ready tasks. In second step, Static Voltage and Frequency Scaling (SVFS) is performed in which, starting from the number of processors determined by MPSched in 1 st step, the operating frequency is scaled down to determine an energy profile of MPSoC. We observe that doing so permits to optimize on energy by approximately 15% even when the computation resource is doubled (Table -3). This gain is observed when all tasks execute with their WCET, i.e. in worst case analysis. The gain on energy will increase when tasks will execute with their actual execution time (which is mostly the case). However, gains will vary with different feature size technologies. Our current and future work will focus on integrating Dynamic Power Management (DPM) and Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) techniques in this framework.
